primary_questions.Q1: After you run a command from a nushell plugin, the plugin's process is kept alive for reuse rather than shut down immediately. What decides when an idle plugin finally gets stopped, and which code actually stops the process?
primary_questions.Q2: When a user presses Ctrl-C while a long-running nushell pipeline is producing output, how does the code that is running actually notice and stop? What does it check, and where does that shared state live?

holdout_questions.Q2: When a Nushell error updates the last command's exit status, how does it choose between an external program's exit status and a shell error's status, and where does it store the chosen value?
holdout_questions.Q1: How does Nushell prevent a recursive user-defined command from exhausting the native call stack? Identify where the recursion depth is carried and incremented, which configurable limit is checked, and what happens when the limit is exceeded in its evaluators.

reviews.Q1:
Q1 review: all four answers are incomplete under the full rubric; answer-3 and answer-2 additionally contain material factual errors. This is a model-assisted source review, not independent human validation. No files were changed and no tests, builds, lint, formatting, or inference were run.

SHARED REFERENCE FACTS
Paths below are relative to D:/kodlama/bench_repos/nushell. Criterion IDs Q1.1–Q1.5 correspond, in order, to the five Q1 rubric entries. A criterion's met flag means the whole criterion is covered; partial correct coverage is identified in evidence rather than treated as a factual error.

Q1.1 — Configuration: crates/nu-protocol/src/config/plugin_gc.rs:7-19 selects a named plugin configuration or the default; :47-60 defines enabled=true and stop_after=10_000_000_000 ns by default. The configured stop_after replaces the default duration; there is no additional delay field. Inactivity is not process age.
Q1.2 — Usage: crates/nu-plugin-engine/src/interface/mod.rs:797-806 increments a GC lock when starting a call; :539-545 releases it on a successful call response. Output streams acquire/release separate usage locks at :205-235, including response stream registration at :519-529. In crates/nu-plugin-engine/src/gc.rs:113-127, a timeout requires locks<=0, no plugin disable override, enabled config, and an existing last_update. Only AddLocks changes last_update (:141-152). SetConfig only replaces config (:133-135), and SetDisabled only changes disabled (:154-156); neither resets the activity timestamp.
Q1.3 — Scheduling: gc.rs:113-127 calculates max(stop_after - elapsed_since_last_update, 0). The worker waits with recv_timeout when a timeout exists, otherwise recv, and recalculates after processing messages (:169-194); it calls plugin.stop when the remaining timeout reaches zero (:196-213). This is deadline-driven, not a periodic configurable polling interval. Exited DOES cause stop: :161-163 returns Some(true), :183-188 sets always_stop, and :198-207 invokes plugin.stop if the weak reference upgrades. StopTracking is the distinct message that exits without stopping (:157-159,189-191). The engine reader emits Exited when its consume loop ends, at interface/mod.rs:447-450.
Q1.4 — Persistent shutdown: crates/nu-plugin-engine/src/persistent.rs:276-278 implements RegisteredPlugin::stop by calling stop_internal(false). The latter stops the old GC's tracking and clears mutable.running (:236-244), dropping RunningPlugin, whose fields are an interface and GC handle (:53-59). It does not call Child.kill. The persistent interface is what enables reuse (:91-93,224), not a foreground guard.
Q1.5 — Actual graceful-exit chain: the last engine PluginInterface drop calls goodbye at crates/nu-plugin-engine/src/interface/mod.rs:1219-1232; goodbye writes PluginInput::Goodbye and flushes (:660-668). The plugin-side dispatch explicitly consumes Goodbye by dropping its call sender at crates/nu-plugin/src/plugin/interface/mod.rs:339-343. The call_receiver loop then ends, scoped call workers finish, and serve_plugin_io returns (:575-653 in crates/nu-plugin/src/plugin/mod.rs); normal serve_plugin success returns at :367-376. Engine cleanup calls child.wait at crates/nu-plugin-engine/src/init.rs:107-139, via after_close after the reader/manager ends (:175-182), which waits/reaps rather than kills. Dropping a Rust std::process::Child handle does not itself kill or automatically wait for the process: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Child.html. Therefore a summary saying interface disposal allows natural exit is incomplete without the protocol chain, but is not itself a claim that Child destruction kills.

reviews.Q2:
Audit scope: model-assisted review of the four final answers against actual Nushell source; no arm labels inferred, files changed, inference run, or tests/builds executed. Criterion IDs Q2.1–Q2.5 follow rubric order. A met=true judgment recognizes equivalent causal explanations, not mandatory literal keywords; met=false can indicate an omission rather than a contradiction.

SHARED REFERENCE FACTS
Q2.1 — Signals derives Clone and contains Option<Arc<AtomicBool>>; cloning shares the atomic allocation, not its current boolean value (crates/nu-protocol/src/pipeline/signals.rs:12–31). EngineState owns Signals and exposes/sets it (crates/nu-protocol/src/engine/engine_state.rs:109,286–288,316–318).
Q2.2 — ctrlc_protection creates AtomicBool(false), gives EngineState a cloned Arc, and moves the original Arc into the registered callback; Nushell's callback stores true with Relaxed ordering, then runs SignalAction::Interrupt handlers (src/signals.rs:7–33). This callback is not a global Rust unwinder. Separately, one registered handler kills background jobs (src/signals.rs:13–25), so the cooperative explanation should concern the running pipeline's flag checkpoints, not deny every other signal effect.
Q2.3 — interrupted() atomically loads with Relaxed ordering and returns false for an absent flag; check() returns ShellError::Interrupted or Ok(()). The caller must propagate/handle the error or branch on the boolean (crates/nu-protocol/src/pipeline/signals.rs:43–74).
Q2.4 — A concrete producer, generate, passes engine_state.signals().clone() into into_pipeline_data (crates/nu-command/src/generators/generate.rs:126–146). The conversion creates ListStream with those Signals (crates/nu-protocol/src/pipeline/pipeline_data.rs:1081–1103); ListStream::new installs InterruptIter (crates/nu-protocol/src/pipeline/list_stream.rs:22–34). InterruptIter::next returns None when interrupted, otherwise invokes its underlying iterator's next (same file:166–190). This is an actual termination branch, not merely an interrupt-related method name.
Q2.5 — Reader::read propagates a checked interrupt through ShellErrorBridge before calling the underlying read (crates/nu-protocol/src/pipeline/byte_stream.rs:837–842). write_all_and_flush checks before each 8192-byte write and propagates failure (crates/nu-protocol/src/pipeline/pipeline_data.rs:924–957); eval_call checks before evaluating a command (crates/nu-engine/src/eval.rs:343–350). The flag itself does not preempt an underlying blocked read/write or an unchecked loop: control must reach another check. Likewise, InterruptIter checks before entering the underlying next, not continuously while next executes.

Overall: no answer meets every Q2 rubric criterion. The principal failures are omissions, not confidently established critical factual contradictions; small ownership/location/generalization issues are called out separately so they are not confused with invented mechanisms.

sources.lesson: Optimize useful context and complete workflows; measure real task performance and total tokens, not payload size alone.
Keep high-signal context and use just-in-time retrieval; context management is distinct from source selection.
Budget relevant repository navigation, then retrieve needed source.
Sourcegraph documented adapted-BM25 lexical retrieval and global snippet ranking; embeddings are not universally required.

limitations: One local 9B model; four questions in one repository; small sequentially developed pilots, not a broad benchmark.
Do not pool configurations with different output/reasoning settings as one experiment.
No claim that smaller payloads or fewer tools are universally worse. These candidates failed their local acceptance checks.
Baseline directory grep only searches Rust with 40 total hits and 5 per file; findings do not establish superiority against other native toolkits.
No Pi/TUI integration benchmark was run; this exercises the Python loop against actual MCP schemas/text.
Zero fully complete rubric answers prevents a meaningful tokens-per-fully-correct ratio.
Raw artifacts are local and git-ignored; this committed summary retains metrics, source references, review findings and hashes.
